paragraphs.body: It was three hours into her shift before Maggie was able to speak with her favorite coworker. Usually, the gym was empty on the bright, sunny spring days, but today the phone at the membership desk had been going off nonstop, and Carl wasn’t able to join her behind the smoothie bar until noon. By the time he wandered over, Maggie had served a total of two customers and played seventeen rounds of wordle unlimited on the work computer. Sunny days were slow at the gym, but they made everyone want to sign up. Jake, the only trainer on Saturdays, whose classes had all been canceled, had been Maggie’s only companion while she’d desperately watched Carl speak on the phone and pray that he’d be free soon.

annotations.comment: This made me laugh. You put us in this world very nicely.
Maybe “by phone” just to make this clear?
You kind of tell us Jake joins her twice — reduce to just one mention?

annotations.model_comment: You've established a strong foundation for storytelling in your introduction, effectively conveying the monotony of Maggie's workday and her anticipation of interacting with her coworkers. To add greater depth to this opening section, consider incorporating sensory details that immerse readers in the environment of the gym during a typically quiet period. For instance, describe the sounds of soft music playing in the background, the scent of disinfectant wafting through the air, or the warm sunlight streaming through the windows. These small additions can enhance the atmosphere and draw readers into the world you're creating.

paragraphs.body: “About time,” Maggie groaned, as Carl finally slid behind the smoothie bar. “Today has been so boring.”
“Hey,” Jake said playfully. “I’ve been keeping you company the entire time you’ve been here. Am I nothing to you?”
Carl laughed and splayed himself over the countertop, “I literally can’t with this job anymore.”
“It’s really not that bad,” Jake said. “Imagine doing my job.”
Maggie laughed, “What job? All you’ve done all day is give me terrible answers to these puzzles.”
Jake shoved her, “I’m just offering a different perspective.” He took a breath and then looked over at Carl, “Hey speaking of, has Annie decided if she wants to sign up for my classes?”
“Um, I’m not sure. I think she’s just a bit busy right now.” Carl gave Maddie a look that meant he didn’t think Annie wanted to take any classes with Jake ever.

annotations.comment: It’s interesting that the story seems to be more about Jake than Maddie, but we didn’t get a ton of set up about Jake.

annotations.model_comment: To add more depth to your narrative, consider incorporating sensory details throughout the conversation between Carl, Maggie, and Jake. While we get a clear picture of the events unfolding, the interactions often rely heavily on dialogue without providing context or description of the environment, body language, or emotions beyond what's explicitly stated. For example, during Carl's storytelling, you mention "she lived alone" and "her one-bedroom apartment," but we're missing visual cues about the layout, lighting, or atmosphere of the space. Similarly, when describing the tension building inside the protagonist's apartment, you could elaborate on the sounds, smells, or physical sensations that contribute to her growing unease. Fleshing out these aspects will draw readers deeper into the world you've created and enhance the overall impact of the story.

paragraphs.body: “Yeah, no I get it,” Jake persisted. “It’s just, I know that crazy thing happened to her friend, maybe I could teach her self defence or something.”
Maggie looked at Jake. “What crazy thing?”
“Wait, you don’t know?” Jake laughed. “Carl, you’ve told everyone, how does Maggie not know yet?”
Carl gasped, turning towards Maggie “Girl, do I have the story for you.”
“Oh, this is gonna be great.” Jake leaned back against the counter and watched Maggie.

annotations.comment: Yikes! But wouldn’t plastic tarps be more efficient? I enjoyed this story, Claire — it’s almost a ghost story in that it really hinges on believing something that doesn’t quite hold up in the daylight but is undeniably creepy in the moment. To be the part that needs your attention is Carl and Jake (and Maggie). Are they telling her the story just to freak her out? If so, why? Do they sincerely believe this is a true story? (Again, if so — why?) Why would Jake ask Carl to tell her this awful story? IN general, I’d just like a sense of their purpose here, especially since Carl is presented as Maggie’s best friend. Maybe he knows she will (on some level) enjoy the story, but it feels a little sadistic to me. And I wanted some closure there, so tie back to the quiet day and waiting so long for Carl to come over, etc. etc. This sounds a little cranky, I realize, so let me say again that so much here works great! It’s just that fringe 10% that needs work. Thanks, Claire! Happy revising!Grade: A
